summary: Specifies the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol, used between a Path Computation Client and a PCE or between PCEs. It carries path computation requests and replies and notifications for MPLS and GMPLS traffic engineering, and is designed to be extensible. This is a Proposed Standard, extended by many later RFCs.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5440 defines PCEP, a protocol for a client to ask a specialized calculator (a PCE) to find paths through a network, and for that calculator to return the paths that satisfy the requested constraints.

subtitle: A protocol for a Path Computation Element to compute and manage MPLS or GMPLS paths for clients.

tldr.problem: The PCE architecture separates the element that computes a path (the PCE) from the client that needs it (the PCC); when the two are not in the same place they need a protocol to communicate.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5440 defines the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP), a TCP-based protocol between a Path Computation Client (PCC) and a Path Computation Element (PCE), and between two PCEs, to request, reply to and notify path computations.
tldr.outcome: It enables constraint-based path computation in MPLS and GMPLS networks. RFC 5440 has been updated by later RFCs; it does not obsolete any prior RFC.

facts.value: Open, Keepalive, PCReq, PCRep, PCNtf, PCErr, Close

today: RFC 5440 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It has been updated by RFC 7896, RFC 8253, RFC 8356, RFC 9488 and RFC 9756.

sections.title: Background and Motivation
sections.content:
[RFC4655] defines a PCE-based architecture for computing Traffic Engineering Label Switched Paths (TE LSPs) in MPLS and GMPLS networks. It separates the element that computes a path, the Path Computation Element (PCE), from the client that needs one, the Path Computation Client (PCC), and lets PCEs cooperate.

When the PCC and PCE are not on the same node, they need a communication protocol; the same protocol is also required between two PCEs. RFC 5440 defines the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) for this, in line with the requirements in RFC 4657. A PCC uses it to send a request for one or more TE LSPs to the PCE, and the PCE replies with computed paths when it can find some that satisfy the constraints.

PCEP is designed to be extensible so that new messages and objects can be added later.
sections.plainLanguage: MPLS networks plan paths for traffic. The work of computing a path can be done by a separate element called a PCE. PCEP is the language a client uses to ask a PCE for a path and get the answer back.

sections.title: PCE and PCC Roles
sections.content:
A PCC is the client that requests path computation, and a PCE is the server that computes paths. Either may be an MPLS or GMPLS network element; when the two are not on the same node they communicate with PCEP, and two PCEs may also use it with each other.

PCEP operates over TCP, which provides reliable delivery and flow control. PCEP messages are Open and Keepalive (to start and maintain a session), PCReq (a PCC requesting a path computation), PCRep (a PCE replying with computed paths or a negative reply), PCNtf (a notification of a specific event), PCErr (a protocol error) and Close (to end the session).
sections.plainLanguage: The client (PCC) asks for paths. The calculator (PCE) replies with paths that fit the rules, or says why it could not find any. They talk over a reliable TCP connection.

sections.title: Protocol Operations
sections.content:
PCEP operates in request-response mode. A PCC sends a PCReq message containing one or more path computation requests, each specifying the source, destination, constraints and other parameters. The PCE replies with a PCRep message containing computed paths (explicit routes) or indicating failure with reasons.

Both ends exchange Open messages to establish a session, negotiating capabilities and parameters. Keepalive messages maintain liveness. PCErr reports errors, PCNtf provides notifications, and Close ends the session.
sections.plainLanguage: After setting up a session, the client asks for a path with specific constraints. The calculator returns either the path(s) or explains why it can't compute them.

sections.title: Error Handling and Notifications
sections.content:
PCEP uses PCErr messages to report protocol or computation errors, with error codes and optional details. PCNtf messages convey notifications. Errors can occur during session establishment, request processing, or other operations.

The protocol includes mechanisms to handle malformed messages and session termination gracefully. Keepalive ensures sessions don't time out prematurely.
sections.plainLanguage: If something goes wrong, the calculator or client sends an error message explaining the problem. Regular keepalive messages ensure both sides know the connection is still alive.

sections.title: Message Format Overview
sections.content:
Each PCEP message has a common header, and messages carry one or more objects. Objects are encoded using the PCEP TLV format and have their own common object header. The RFC defines objects such as OPEN, RP, NO-PATH, END-POINTS, BANDWIDTH, METRIC, the Explicit Route Object, the Reported Route Object, LSPA, Include Route and SVEC.

The protocol is designed to be flexible and extensible so that further messages and objects can be added as new requirements appear.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages start with a short header and then carry labelled data blocks called objects, such as the endpoints or the bandwidth. New kinds of block can be added later.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
Section 10 of the RFC describes the vulnerabilities of a PCEP session, including attacks on TCP connections and on path computation itself. TCP protection techniques such as TCP-MD5 or TCP-AO are discussed for authentication and integrity.

Privacy can be provided by running TCP over an IPsec tunnel; the RFC notes that IPsec also gives authentication and integrity, but that configuring IPsec at scale can be hard, and leaves detailed use of IPsec with PCEP to separate work. Access policy, rate limiting and shaping are covered as defences against denial of service.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol itself doesn't encrypt messages by default. In practice, operators protect the connection with additional security layers like IPsec.
